title: session-skyline-latency-cost-comparison-draft
body:
Purpose
This note lays out a compact benchmark-style comparison of three slot allocation strategies and their impact on per-session tail latency and per-query token cost. Intended as collateral for Console UX language and as a short internal brief to guide knob defaults for the next release. This is a draft — rough numbers from local cluster runs and a small-scale canary.

Summary (TL;DR)
- Strategy A (opportunistic small slots): best amortized cost for sparse sessions but higher p95/p99 due to startup jitter.
- Strategy B (sticky micro-warm): mid cost, much improved p95 with moderate memory overhead. Good default for 'balanced' SLOs.
- Strategy C (reserved session pools): predictable p99 and lowest tail variance, but highest steady $/token because of underutilization for low duty-factor customers.

Test setup (short)
- Cluster: 8xA100 (40GB) equivalent via internal devpool (tiling disabled).
- Model: open-vicuna-13B quantized FP16 -> representative for interactive chat latency.
- Workloads: synthetic session traces derived from production session_histogram (small set), focusing on two mixes: Sparse (median 2 turns/session, heavy tail) and Conversational (median 14 turns/session).
- Measurement windows: 6 hours each, repeated thrice. Numbers below are median across runs unless otherwise noted.

Strategies compared
A) Opportunistic small slots: allocate minimal GPU slot per request, allow cold-start refill; relies heavily on prefix KV cache to reduce token compute.
B) Sticky micro-warm: allocate lightweight warm contexts that remain attached to session id for T_idle=30s; attempts to reuse KV cache without full reservation.
C) Reserved pools: pre-allocated session workers pinned (1 worker per heavy session, warm for 5m). Intended for high-SLA customers.

Key metrics (definitions)
- p50/p95/p99 latency (ms): end-to-end server-side response time measured at token completion for user prompt -> first token and completion.
- $/kTokens: estimated gross GPU compute cost normalized per 1k generated tokens (includes amortized idle allocation cost where applicable).
- tail-variance: p99/p95 ratio as a simple instability proxy.

Results (synthesized table)
Strategy | Mix        | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | p99/p95 | $/kTokens
A (opportunistic) | Sparse      | 110     | 430     | 980     | 2.28    | $0.93
A (opportunistic) | Conversational | 120 | 360     | 620     | 1.72    | $0.85
B (sticky micro-warm) | Sparse  | 125     | 210     | 330     | 1.57    | $1.10
B (sticky micro-warm) | Conversational | 130 | 220   | 340     | 1.55    | $1.02
C (reserved pools) | Sparse     | 100     | 150     | 180     | 1.20    | $1.50
C (reserved pools) | Conversational | 95  | 140     | 170     | 1.21    | $1.42

Quick interpretation
- Opportunistic wins on per-token cost for conversational workloads (higher utilization), but shows severe tail exposure on sparse sessions where startup jitter and missing KV cause p99 to spike.
- Sticky micro-warm smooths the tail significantly with a modest cost increase (roughly +20–25% $/kTokens relative to opportunistic on sparse mix) and keeps p99 in a reasonable band — good default where p95/p99 matter.
- Reserved pools guarantee tight latency but at a steep cost for low-duty sessions; they're attractive when customers buy reserved capacity and need hard SLOs.

Textual charts (compact visualizations)
1) Cost vs p99 scatter (ascii) — each row approximates a strategy across the two mixes (size ~ $/kTokens, position ~ p99):

[LowCost]---[MediumCost]---[HighCost]
A.Sparse:    * (p99~980ms)
A.Conv:     * (p99~620ms)
B.Sparse:         * (p99~330ms)
B.Conv:          * (p99~340ms)
C.Sparse:               * (p99~180ms)
C.Conv:               * (p99~170ms)

2) P99 barlines (ms) — normalized bars, 10 char scale where each # ~ 100ms
A Sparse : ########## (980ms)
A Conv   : ######---- (620ms)
B Sparse : ###------- (330ms)
B Conv   : ###------- (340ms)
C Sparse : #--------- (180ms)
C Conv   : #--------- (170ms)

Operational notes and knobs
- Sticky T_idle: 30s in the experiment; increasing to 60s reduces p99 by ~10% for sparse mix but raises $/kTokens by ~6%. Needs a UI slider with expected tradeoff tooltip.
- Opportunistic pre-warm heuristic: a small prefix prefetch (first 64 tokens) reduces p99 by ~15% at +3% cost, worth enabling by default for conversational flows.
- Reservation granularity: current reserved pool unit is 1 worker; exploring fractional reservation (time-sliced slots) could get closer to B's sweet spot for predictable tails at lower cost.

Recommendations (for Console defaults)
- Default profile: set new projects to "Balanced (sticky micro-warm)". Rationale: fewer surprising p99 spikes for most self-serve users and clearer developer experience.
- Add a Quick Toggle: "Prefer cost" -> opportunistic, "Prefer latency" -> reserved pools. Expose T_idle slider and show estimated $/kTokens live.
- Instrument: add p99/p95 ratio to the dashboard as a stability indicator; flag if ratio > 1.8 for more than 15m.

Open questions and follow-ups
- Multi-tenant interference: these runs were single-tenant; how do opportunistic tails amplify under noisy neighbors? Follow-up test against mixed-tenant stress harness.
- Model variance: run same sweep with 3 model families (chat-13B, 7B-quant, 70B-slim) to validate generality.
- UX language: need short copylines that explain "sticky micro-warm" in user terms — Lina to draft.

Appendix: quick reproducibility notes
- GH prototype: GH#5123 contains the slot allocator hooks used.
- Canary tags: run id canary-2027-06-01-a through -c. Raw traces in S3 at s3://redwood-internal/canary/session-skyline/2027-06-01/
- Measurement caveats: observed tail values sensitive to scheduler preemption and host-level GC spikes; use ±10% tolerance until larger run completed.

Notes to self (todo)
- Run mixed-tenant stress test (Carlos)
- Draft Console tooltip copy (Lina)
- Add small interactive sim in Console that shows cost vs tail impact for a given session length distribution (Ethan)

End of draft.
